The house romanization in two registers: the full spelling (workbench, one letter or digraph per sound, tone marks) and the book spelling (lossy: no tone, plain vowels, and at most 2 diacritic letters kept for the whole language; one spelling per sound in every word). ## Grammar

Basic word order is VSO; it has both prepositions and postpositions. In the noun phrase: possessed before the possessor; noun before the adjective; noun before the demonstrative; numeral before the noun; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-initial.
It has a definite article after the noun, no indefinite article, no case marking on nouns, no alignment marking (subject and object are not told apart by form), no grammatical number, a gender system based on sex.
Verbs mark past and perfective; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a clause-initial negator; yes/no questions use a final question particle. Verbs do not agree with their arguments.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; serial verbs; adjectives that behave like verbs; a periphrastic causative; a periphrastic passive; question words left in place.
Measured morphology: 10 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 0.3 (0 free word … 3 fused), 0 paradigm cells, 0 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns have no case marking. Subject and object are not marked apart: word order tells them. Place and company are said with the plain words 'in' (l‼u˦ɡu˨), 'at' (i˨ji˨), 'with' (i˨jwi˨) as adpositions.

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns fall into genders by sex: class 1 for men, and by default most other nouns, a clitic after the noun (sɛ˦kʷl‼i˦, from 'man'); class 2 for women and female beings, a separate word after the noun (kʷa˨zi˦, from 'woman').

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a clitic before the verb (ɡo˨˯zwe˦, from 'yesterday'); perfect (PRF): a clitic before the verb (la˨zi˨˯, from 'finish'). Unmarked: future, progressive, habitual (left to context).

**Person agreement.** Verbs do not agree with the subject. Short unstressed pronouns stand beside the verb (2SG kʷa˦), on their way to becoming agreement.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are two themes from a closed pool, compounded (as Germanic *Wil-helm*, Slavic *Vladi-mir*); the byname is the father's name in the genitive with 'son' or 'daughter'. The tradition goes back to the white dragon proto-language. Themes: first eagle, good, holy, land, star, strong, war, wolf; second gift, head, heart, master, mind, stone.

| name | IPA | meaning | | etymology |

| **Somh** | /so˨˯/ | 'star-head' | old | Somh 'star-head': omh 'star' + somh 'head'; an old name, coined in d116 4.0 kyr ago as Soomh |
| **Lrhazdzugu** | /l‼a˦zɖʐu˦ɡu˨/ | 'good-master' | old | Lrhazdzugu 'good-master': dzugu 'good' + lrhaze 'master'; an old name, coined in d116 4.0 kyr ago as Lrhazedzugu |
| **Galrromh** | /ɡa˨lro˦˯/ | 'wolf-stone' | old | Galrromh 'wolf-stone': lomh 'wolf' + gala 'stone'; an old name, coined in d116 4.0 kyr ago as Galalomh |
| **Golrhḷowdzugu** | /ɡɔ˨l‼ɭɔ˨wɖʐu˦ɡu˨/ | 'good-gift' | new | Golrhḷowdzugu 'good-gift': dzugu 'good' + golrhḷowswimhwe 'gift'; coined from today's words |
| **Kwikwziyyrhe** | /kʷi˨kʷzi˨jj‼e˨/ | 'eagle-heart' | new | Kwikwziyyrhe 'eagle-heart': ziyyrhe 'eagle' + kwikwi 'heart'; coined from today's words |

**Settlements.** **Larrgagai** /la˨rɡa˨ɡa˨i˨/ (town, 6,525): 'Barhidarhlaerh's fence'; named by the kobold (d440) who founded it 1.2 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Larrgazi** /la˨rɡa˨zi˨/ (town, 3,281): 'the long fence'; named by the kobold (d440) who founded it 0.7 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Iylrhilrre** /i˨jl‼i˨lrɛ˨/ (town, 1,859): 'I'iolobeo's market'; town + the old name: 'town I'iolobeo's market' (a tautology, like River Avon); named by the kobold (d440) who founded it 1.2 kyr ago, kept as heard.

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

**(1)** ‘The woman sees the dog.’

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
